title: Why he avoided steady quarter-note bass drum; Zutty's New Orleans style
summary: Crouch notes Greer rarely played four-to-the-bar bass drum; Greer says it was intuition and Duke never told him what to play.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah, you played with him for -- well, Zootie played--the style of drums he played was just a little bit before you came through?
He played strictly the New Orleans drum style.
Yeah, a lot of press rolls?
Yeah.

Well, you know, one of the things I wanted to ask you about your style of drumming, I forgot to ask you. Now, you know how like--(unintelligible). Most of the other drummers -- I listen to you a lot on records and most of the drummers would always play quarter notes for the bass player. You know, it would be boom, boom, boom, boom, boom (humming.) But I noticed on a lot of the records you play on, you're not playing that.
No, no. I played that sometimes but not continuously, you know. It depends on what we were playing, you know, that sort. You know, that's fine. A lot of guys got away from it now, you know.
Quarter notes?
Uh-huh. I don't know, man. I play
just usually with the piano. We played concerts like that.
You and Brooks Kerr?
Yeah. You know. And I don't know, intuition. Just a feel of it.
Well, did you get -- was it that you -- that sound, did you find it too repetitious or boring? Or you just heard something else you wanted to play?
No, it never bored me. I used to like to hear the guys play it.
No, I'm talking about for you. I'm not talking about them.
I don't know, it didn't bore me. I was so busy enjoying it, I never got bored, man.

Oh, no, I don't mean bored while you were playing. I'm talking about like -- you know, that's a distinctly different thing about your style of drumming and other drummers, you know, in theory. Because very rarely do you play that quarter note bass drum figure. I mean Chick Webb and a lot of other guys I've heard on records, you listen to them and they'd be playing a bass drum (humming). But you put on Duke Ellington's band, boomp, boomp, boomp ain't going on.
No.
And I was just trying to find out what --
I don't know.
You didn't remember?
No. Man, I don't know. Duke had so many ideas.
Did he suggest that you not play it all the time?

No, he never. He left -- he never told me to play this or that. He would leave it up to my intuition. He never -- I'd play. I'd just look, you know, I'd play along with the guys and I'd just feel different things that fit different guys.
Oh, so you would adapt what you were playing to whether or not you thought it would fit the guy that was playing?
Yeah. Or fit the number he was playing.
So if a particular guy was playing, was improvising at some point, you would -- if you thought that the bass drum figures went with his style of playing, and if they didn't you'd cancel?
Oh, yeah. Yeah, if it didn't go. You never hear that no more. Never hear that stuff no more.
